2	
3	SYNTHETIC EVALUATION MATERIAL. This is the entire fictional source package. Source language: English. No external facts or quotations may be added.
4	
5	## Brief
6	
7	Write a journalistic customer case for operations managers at small housing companies. The publisher is the supplier, Svale Systems. The customer, Elm Quay Housing, should remain the acting party. Approximately 400 words, as material allows. Markdown. No author name supplied. The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial.
8	
9	## Material
10	
11	Elm Quay Housing manages 640 flats. In September 2025 its own maintenance team decided to trial a shared repair log in two buildings. Previously telephone reports and emails were stored separately. The team wanted staff on different shifts to see the same information. It chose Svale Systems after testing whether the log could show the status of each repair. No comparison with another supplier is available.
12	
13	The maintenance team designed its categories and kept telephone reporting open for residents. Svale configured the log and trained six staff during two sessions. The trial lasted eight weeks. Elm Quay's internal trial note, 4 December 2025, says that 31 repair reports were entered. It excludes emergencies and work ordered before the trial. Median time from report to assignment was two working days during the trial and three in the preceding eight-week period. The periods had different workloads, and the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software. There are no cost, resident-satisfaction or completion-time measurements.
14	
15	Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind, complete usable quotations:
16	
17	- “We wanted the evening shift to see what the morning shift had already done. The categories were ours; Svale helped us put them into the log.”
18	- “We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts.”
19	- “I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation.”
20

The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs. The supplier approved publication of this case as supplier-published material; it is not independent journalism. All interviews occurred by email, and no physical scene, emotion or remembered dialogue is provided. Translation of the quotations is permitted, preserving stance and qualification.
22

1	## Claims
2	
3	Every claim is supported by the text or its material, with exact attribution and proportionate strength. Preserve the state of knowledge: what is unknown or unclaimed is not thereby known not to have happened. Keep uncertainty where it exists and certainty where it is warranted. A fact, quotation, source, scene, personal experience or opinion attributed to somebody is never invented to complete a form. Name the actual source of an attributed claim rather than invoking unnamed studies or experts.
4	
5	Circumstantial detail is a claim too: duration, manner, motive, absence and background all need support. So does an evaluative characterisation: calling a count high, low or modest needs a comparison, target, capacity or speaker assessment. Otherwise give the count with its exclusions, without that assessment.
6	
7	A sequence or correlation establishes no cause. A causal verb such as *shortened* needs causal support; a causal hedge such as *suggests that it shortened* still adds that attribution. This boundary holds in the title, summary, headings and body alike. Preserve chronology, scope and qualifications wherever a claim appears.
8	
9	A stated length constrains the use of material and is never a licence to add to it. When the material is insufficient, deliver the length the material supports and name what further material would close the gap. A supplied publication limit is binding; meeting it cannot justify invention or loss of a qualification that changes a claim.
10

1	# Quoting speech
2	
3	Read this before putting quotation marks around anything somebody said. It applies to interview transcripts, recorded remarks, meeting notes, and any other material where the words are a person's rather than a document's.
4	
5	Speech is not written prose, and a transcript quoted raw reads as carelessness towards the speaker rather than fidelity to them. So a spoken quotation may be repaired — cautiously, within a boundary that is easier to state than to feel your way to.
6	
7	When translating permitted quotations, preserve meaning, stance, certainty and distinctive voice in idiomatic target-language speech, not source-language syntax. The restrictions below protect that substance; they do not require word-for-word translation. Make an implicit referent explicit only when the supplied context settles it. Where the meaning remains ambiguous, paraphrase what is established rather than inventing a fluent interpretation.
8	
9	## What may be repaired
10	
11	The syntax of speech: a sentence abandoned halfway and restarted, a subject left behind by its verb, a clause that never closes. Fillers — *you know*, *sort of*, *liksom*, *alltså* — where they carry nothing. Repetition that is the speaker searching for a word rather than insisting on one. False starts, and the small disfluencies a person does not hear themselves make.
12	
13	That is the whole list. Everything on it is noise the speaker did not intend to produce, and removing it leaves what they meant to say.
14	
15	## What may not
16	
17	**Meaning.** Not narrowed, not widened, not sharpened. A speaker who said *most of them* has not said *all of them*, and one who said *we looked at it* has not said *we rejected it*.
18	
19	**Stance.** Approval stays approval, reluctance stays reluctance, and a speaker who was careful not to blame anybody is not made to blame somebody by a tidier sentence.
20	
21	**Certainty.** *I think*, *probably*, *as far as I know*, and *we are not sure yet* are the claim, not padding on it. Removing a hedge manufactures a confidence the speaker did not have; adding one takes away a confidence they did.
22	
23	**Distinctive wording.** Where the speaker reached for an unusual word, an image, a piece of slang, or a phrasing that is theirs, it stays. Smoothing it into the register of the surrounding article is the most tempting of these failures and the one a reader can least detect.
24	
25	**A self-correction.** Where a speaker gives a number or a fact and then corrects it, the correction is what they said. Quoting the first version is a misquotation; quoting a version that never existed — the correction with the correcting away — is worse.
26	
27	**Anything additive.** Add no new meaning: no fact, stance, certainty, name, figure or connection that the speaker did not supply. A permitted repair or translation may change words only to render that same meaning.
28	
29	## When to paraphrase instead
30	
31	Where fidelity is uncertain, paraphrase. A paraphrase that attributes carefully — *she said the change had taken about a year, and that she was not sure it would hold* — is accurate, useful, and honest about what the material supports. A fluent direct quotation assembled out of a fragmentary answer is none of those things, however good it sounds.
32	
33	The cases that should turn into paraphrase: material that is a summary of what somebody said rather than their words; a transcript too broken to repair inside the boundary above; several remarks that would have to be welded together to make one sentence; and any moment where you find yourself choosing between two readings of what the speaker meant.
34	
35	Signal what the material actually is. Where the source is notes rather than a recording, the text says what the person said and does not pretend to their exact wording.
36	
37	## What stays outside this
38	
39	Whether the speaker approves the quotation. Quote approval is a human arrangement between the writer and the person quoted, and nothing here verifies it or stands in for it. A draft may say a quotation is unapproved; it may not treat the absence of approval as a problem it has solved.

    Supported.

    S: "The trial has not yet expanded; the team will decide after checking how the categories work for larger repairs."
    This is a compressed heading, and the next sentence states the exact condition. No decision is made and no expansion occurs before the check, so "any expansion waits" holds. Defensible. Not a finding.

    S: as in item 25.
    Supported. "Its" is neuter and refers to the team, whose categories they are ("The maintenance team designed its categories").

    S (brief): "The optional next step is the supplied implementation checklist at https://example.invalid/svale/checklist; it is a document to read, not a consultation booking or a product trial."
    The link text and verb describe the destination accurately. Supported.

### Checked and not findings

- No causal claim, no claim about savings or resident satisfaction, and no conversion of assignment time into completion time appears anywhere, including the title and headings.
- The brief says the case is supplier-published and not independent journalism. The draft makes no claim of independence. Whether to disclose this is an editorial matter outside this comparison.

## Findings (source support)

### F1. The heading widens what the note declines to credit (moderate)

- Draft: "The trial note stops short of crediting the software"
- Source: "the note explicitly does not attribute the difference to the software."
- Difference in scope and stance: the source limits the non-attribution to "the difference", meaning the change in median assignment time. The heading says the note does not credit the software at all. "Stops short" also suggests the note came close to crediting it, but the source says the note "explicitly" does not.
- Case: the note credits the software with making reports visible to both shifts, while it explicitly declines to attribute the shorter median to it. The source statement holds and the heading fails. No supplied statement rules this out, because the material reports only some of the note's content.
- Smallest repair: "The trial note does not credit the software with the difference"

### F2. "With one change" asserts that there was only one change (low)

- Draft (standfirst): "why the maintenance supervisor would run the trial again with one change."
- Source: "I would choose to do the trial again. Having one view of the reports helps us, but I would leave an extra week for preparation."
- Difference in scope: Lind names one thing she would do differently. The draft says one change is all she would make.
- Case: Lind would repeat the trial with an extra preparation week and also with other changes she was not asked about. Her quotation holds and "with one change" fails. Nothing in the material says the extra week is her only change.
- Smallest repair: "...would run the trial again with more time for preparation."

### F3. "Where the preparation time went" goes beyond the comparison in the quotation (low)

- Draft: "Lind points to where the preparation time went:"
- Source: "We spent more time agreeing on the categories than entering the first reports. I would set that time aside before the next building starts."
- Difference in the thing measured: Lind compares the time spent agreeing categories with the time spent entering the first reports. The lead-in presents the quotation as an account of how the preparation time was divided, which implies that categories took most of it. The material does not say how preparation time was split among category work, configuration and the two training sessions.
- Case: configuration and training took more of the preparation than category agreement, yet agreeing categories still took longer than entering the first reports. The quotation holds and the lead-in's implication fails. No supplied statement rules this out.
- Smallest repair: "Lind compares the work on categories with entering the first reports:"

### F4. The definite title makes Lind the only maintenance supervisor (low)

- Draft: "Elm Quay's maintenance supervisor, Maya Lind" (opening); "the maintenance supervisor" (standfirst)
- Source: "Customer interview with maintenance supervisor Maya Lind"
- Difference in number: the source gives Lind's role but not whether she is the only person in it. The possessive appositive and the definite standfirst present her as Elm Quay's sole maintenance supervisor.
- Case: Elm Quay, which manages 640 flats, has more than one maintenance supervisor. The source holds and the draft's wording fails. No supplied statement rules this out.
- Smallest repair: in the opening, "described by maintenance supervisor Maya Lind"; in the standfirst, "why maintenance supervisor Maya Lind would run the trial again..." (or "an Elm Quay maintenance supervisor").

## Translation findings

None. The source and the draft are both in English, and the three quotations match the source word for word.

## Completion status

Complete. All claims in the title, standfirst, headings, body, quotations and link were accounted for. Unresolved findings: F1 (moderate), F2, F3, F4 (low). No editorial questions remain open.
